extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers (graduate students, postdocs, faculty) writing grant proposals
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for preparing competitive, fundable research grant proposals (general across federal agencies and foundations), covering structure (esp. the one-page specific aims), writing clarity, interpersonal/professional considerations, and how to respond to reviews and resubmit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the instructions / compliance with submission rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Thoroughly read and comply with the funder’s instructions (page limits, section headings, required tables, minimum fonts, maximum margins, reference styles, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violating instructions can cause immediate rejection or bias reviewers against you; electronic submission systems sometimes enforce compliance but do not guarantee safety from all noncompliance. Before writing, download and read instructions (maybe twice) and then COMPLY!

rubrics_metrics.name: Align proposal content to funder's goals and reviewer criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Include sections the instructions request (e.g., innovation, diversity relevance) because instructions often mirror reviewer evaluation criteria and funder mission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If instructions ask about specific themes, reviewers will likely be scored on those themes—address them explicitly so reviewers can find and score your work accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generate reviewer 'excitement' and communicate importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond being free of fatal flaws, proposals should create genuine excitement — make reviewers care early about your research questions and why answers matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid proposals that merely 'tweak paradigms' (unlikely to excite) and avoid overpromising or grandiosity. Use engaging framing, highlight interesting anomalies or novel connections, and get the reader thinking about the key questions quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get to the point quickly / frontload the core question
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliver your main research question and the 'good part' early so reviewers' short attention fuse is ignited quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid lengthy lead-ins that delay the core point; obscuring the research question risks losing reviewer interest during their limited attention window.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific aims: one-page clarity, comprehensiveness, and concision
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft a one-page specific-aims section that states the problem, explains its importance, sketches methods, lists hypotheses, and touches on significance—be comprehensive yet strictly one page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The one-page limit forces you to reveal weaknesses in logic, vagueness in methods, or weak rationale; rewrite the aims many times until they are clear, complete, cogent, and compelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specific aims as the proposal framework and feedback instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop the specific-aims page first to refine logic and then use it to solicit rapid feedback from colleagues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most successful scientists will read and comment on a one-page aims page; iterate multiple times with colleagues before writing the full proposal. The aims page will be used by reviewers, program staff, and others to summarize your project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect rejection; be prepared to revise and resubmit
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate that many proposals will fail initially; use reviews and resubmission opportunities as the primary path to eventual funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read reviews carefully, learn from them, and plan for multiple submission cycles. Do not let initial failure cause paralysis; view reviews as lifelines that indicate how to improve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond productively to reviews; avoid solipsistic myopia
rubrics_metrics.description: When you receive critiques, avoid reflexively blaming reviewers or convincing yourself they were biased; instead, seek objective interpretation and prioritize revisions indicated by reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show reviews to experienced colleagues who can read between the lines and help determine which issues are real and what level of revision is needed (minor edits vs. starting over). Gauge whether reviewers signaled excitement or boredom to decide next steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remember grants are reviewed by people — mind interpersonal consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Because human reviewers evaluate proposals, manage tone and relationships: avoid ad hominem remarks, scathing critiques of named researchers, or unnecessarily antagonistic language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume zero degrees of separation—reviewers may be connected to people you criticize. Temper criticisms to avoid alienating reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid absolute claims of primacy / overclaiming novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assert that 'nobody before you has done X'—such claims invite quick counterexamples and charges of sloppy scholarship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully explain how your work differs from prior work without making sweeping claims of firstness; be precise and modest about novelty claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide sufficient background and context for outsiders (avoid silo assumptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume reviewers share your insider knowledge; include critical details about past studies, theories, controversies, and findings so reviewers from other subfields can follow your logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to provide context risks charges of 'hand-waving' and 'name-dropping'—give clear descriptions of prior studies and how they relate to your project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be humble — present advantages and disadvantages candidly
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid grandiose claims about your theory or methods; acknowledge limitations and treat alternative approaches respectfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A measured approach that outlines pros/cons of your methods and recognizes others' work is more likely to persuade reviewers than arrogance or exaggerated claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and simplicity of writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Write with absolute clarity—there is no such thing as a paragraph in a grant that is too clear; unclear writing equals unclear thinking to reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for simple, direct prose so reviewers do not need to parse or re-read; clarity helps convey ideas effectively and supports perceived credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid jargon; define technical terms for non-specialists
rubrics_metrics.description: Because reviewers often come from different subfields, avoid specialized jargon or define terms when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If critical points depend on specialized vocabulary, provide clear definitions; otherwise, omit jargon to increase accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit abbreviations and use evocative ones sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviations save space but burden reviewers' memory—use only widely-recognized abbreviations or a very small set of memorable ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overuse of custom abbreviations risks losing the thread of your argument when reviewers read multiple applications back-to-back.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct grammar and spelling (avoid signals of carelessness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors in grammar and spelling are often taken as signs of personal carelessness and can bias reviewers against funding your proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use spell-checkers and proofreading; clean polished prose supports reviewers' confidence in your professionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat the written proposal as your primary representative
rubrics_metrics.description: Because you often will not have an opportunity to present or defend your proposal in person, the written words are the main vehicle for representing your ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft your text carefully: structure, clarity, tone, and precision matter because reviewers will rely on the written proposal to understand and evaluate your work.
